concepts.title: Ecology and Society: A Two-Way Relationship

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ecology and Society: A Two-Way Relationship' refers to.
questions.a: Ecology studies how living beings relate to their habitat, and human society is deeply ecological: it draws materials from nature and returns wastes to it. The relationship runs both ways -- environments shape what societies can do, while societies transform environments, increasingly at planetary scale.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ecology and Society: A Two-Way Relationship'.
questions.a: Society lives inside an ecosystem -- taking, transforming and returning -- and both sides reshape the other.

concepts.title: Major Environmental Problems and Their Social Roots

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Major Environmental Problems and Their Social Roots' refers to.
questions.a: Today's ecological troubles -- resource depletion, pollution, loss of species, and climate change -- are not accidents of nature alone: they flow from how societies produce, consume and distribute. Their severity tracks scale of extraction and inequality of exposure, since the poor usually suffer environmental damage first and worst.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Major Environmental Problems and Their Social Roots'.
questions.a: Ecological crisis has a social address -- production systems and unequal power produce both the damage and its victims.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Major Environmental Problems and Their Social Roots' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: kesy203.txt lines 130-280 (resource depletion, pollution, declining biodiversity, climate change, social causes and unequal impacts))

concepts.title: Voices from the Margins: Environmental Movements in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Voices from the Margins: Environmental Movements in India' refers to.
questions.a: Indian environmentalism has grown from livelihood struggles, not leisure concerns. Movements like the Chipko defence of forests, struggles against large dams such as the Narmada campaign, and fishworkers' protests defend access to nature for the poor and question a development model that counts dams and factories but not displaced lives.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Voices from the Margins: Environmental Movements in India'.
questions.a: For the poor, environment is livelihood -- India's green movements are struggles over forests, water and home.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Voices from the Margins: Environmental Movements in India' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Environment and Development: Security for Whom

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Environment and Development: Security for Whom' refers to.
questions.a: Sociology reframes environmental debate as a question of distribution: growth models that promise national wealth may transfer nature's costs to villages, tribes and future generations. Sustainable pathways therefore demand not just technology but changed institutions -- who decides, who pays, who is heard.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Environment and Development: Security for Whom'.
questions.a: Environmental protection is a question of justice -- deciding who bears the costs of growth and who counts in the decision.
